# The dispatcher taking the call site's static arguments: sized in a shadow

**The answer.** The generic dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments; only its arms ignore them. Making each generic arm use the dispatcher's own static parameters is one file, one edited function and three new helpers: 43 code lines in `OverloadSet.java`, plus 1 for the switch and 3 for the variant that leaves generic arms out of a dispatcher that has no static parameters. `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`. The compiler prelude is byte-identical. The 43 compiler tests that declare generic overloads all print the same. Of the 34 that link, 31 have byte-identical classes and 3 differ only inside a generic dispatcher. Top-level functions only: generic dotted methods fail the same way and are not covered (`ScopeMethod`). Enforced, the specification's overload sentence refuses 179 declaration pairs in the library's apis under the narrower reading, 11 of them already errors today, and 6 gated compiler tests; a text scan finds 6 gated interpreter tests (§5).

## 1. How the compiled path handles generics today

- A **static argument** is the type that fills a generic's static parameter at one use. In `grab[\Blue\](b)` it is `Blue`. Usually nobody writes it: the checker infers it from the declared types at the call, so `b: Tag[\Blue\]` gives `X = Blue` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:912-930`).
- An **instantiation** is the generic with its static parameters replaced by static arguments: `grab[\Blue\]` is an instantiation of `grab[\X\]`.
- The compiler writes one *template* class per generic function, with `X` left in the names of the types it mentions (`Marker⟦X⟧`). The class loader stamps an instantiation from it when a class named with real arguments is first needed. For `grab⟦Blue⟧` it copies the template and rewrites every `X` in it to `Blue` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`, `MethodInstantiater.java`). The part of the name after `✚`, the template's arrow type, is never rewritten (`InstantiationMap.java:354`).
- A call that needs no choice at run time is compiled as a call to that named class. The checker's static arguments go straight into the name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`), so `grab(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` calls `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`.
- **Dispatch** is choosing at run time which declaration of an overloaded name runs, by the argument's actual type. A **dispatcher** is the method the compiler generates for that. It tests the argument against each declaration, most specific first, and calls the first that applies (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1303-1760`). One is generated for a declaration when some more specific declaration of the same name may apply at run time. If the least specific declaration is generic, the dispatcher is itself a template, named and loaded like any generic function: `grab⟦Blue⟧` at the call site (`OverloadSet.java:2005-2062`).
- **RTTI** (run-time type information) is the object every compiled value carries that describes its type. That includes the argument of each generic supertype, one per generic name: `Mixed`'s RTTI says `Sub` of `Red` and `Tag` of `Blue`.
- How a generic arm finds its static arguments today: it asks the value for its RTTI (`getRTTI`), asks that for the argument at the arm's generic (`Sub__1()`, giving `Red`), and passes the answer to `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass`. That call spells the instance's name from the RTTI's own Java class (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`, `runtimeValues/RTTI.java:53-58`), and the loader stamps it (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`). Inside a dispatcher template the arms do this too: they ignore the template's `X`, which the loader has already set to the call site's argument (`javap-excerpts.txt:60-80`).
- The authors weighed the question in a comment: "Some overloads have static args, but even if they are supplied, runtime inference is still necessary (so I think) -- drc 2010-02-24 / Not quite so -- if each static parameter is mentioned in any invariant occurrence, then the supplied type is exact" (`OverloadSet.java:1981-1990`).

## 2. The design

**What the specification says.** Declarations of one name share their static parameters (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105`), so "static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`:106-107`). The chapter assumes "that all static variables in functional calls have been instantiated or inferred" (`:136-138`), and they are "statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`expressions/var-ref.tex:37-40`). One set of static arguments, fixed at the call, therefore applies to every declaration. A declaration applies at run time if the value's type is a subtype of its parameter type at those arguments. For `MieDispatchSub`, `grab(b)` with `b: Tag[\Blue\]` fixes `X = Blue`. `Mixed` is not a `Sub[\Blue\]`, so the `Tag` declaration runs and the answer is `Marker[Blue]`.

**`MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a)`, `a: Any`.** The specification refuses the program: `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `grab(a: Any)` is an error "for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them" (`overloading.tex:103-105`). The question of which declaration runs therefore does not arise. If the sentence is not enforced, both readings give the same answer. The call was resolved to `grab(Any)`, which has no static parameters, so the call site supplies none. With no arguments to instantiate it, the generic declaration is not applicable. The code should refuse the pair at compile time (§5). Failing that, it should leave the generic arm out of such a dispatcher, which is the `skip` variant below. Either way `grab(a)` returns the `Any` declaration's `Red`.

**The three candidates.**
- **(a) The dispatcher gains the static arguments as parameters**, and every call site the checker resolved with static arguments pushes their RTTIs. This changes the signature of every dispatcher whose least specific declaration is generic, and the descriptor at every call site that reaches one. The template would then carry `X` twice, in its name and in its parameters. The arms would still be stamped through `loadClosureClass` from RTTI names, which keeps the `ZZ32` naming defect (§4). For `grab(Any)` it passes nothing, because that call site has nothing to pass. Not built.
- **(b) The call site loads an instantiated dispatcher named with the static arguments.** It already does, for every dispatcher that is a template (§1). The change is inside the template: each generic arm whose static parameters match the dispatcher's, up to renaming, is renamed into the dispatcher's parameters. It is then tested with a plain `instanceof Sub⟦X⟧` and called as `grab⟦X⟧` by name, and the loader turns both into `Blue`. Nothing is read from the value, and no signature, call site or template kind changes. This is the specification's model, one instantiation of the name fixed at the call, and it is the smallest of the three. Built.
- **(c) The arms keep reading from the value and skip on mismatch.** The template would need `X`'s RTTI in its body. A generic object's RTTI class reads its parameters' RTTIs from fields (`CodeGen.java:5686-5690`), but a function template has no such field, so this needs a new way to name it. Each arm would then compare the RTTI read from the value with it. Equality is wrong where `X` occurs only covariantly, because the value's argument can be a subtype of the call site's. The correct test is "read ⊑ call site" followed by instantiating at the call site's argument, and that is (b) with the reading left in. It changes every generic arm of every template dispatcher, keeps `loadClosureClass`, and keeps both defects of §4. Not built.

## 3. The size, measured

**The shadow** (`scope/scope-shadow.patch`, first file): `OverloadSet.java` only. In `generateCall` (`:1303`), a generic arm of a template dispatcher gets a `StaticTypeReplacer` from its static parameters to the dispatcher's (`atTemplateParams`). Its parameter and return types are built at those parameters, so they contain no variable of the arm's and take the existing no-inference path. The call goes to the arm's instance named with the dispatcher's parameters (`invokeArmAtTemplateParams`: the same stem the value-reading path passes to `loadClosureClass`, with the arm's name moved away from the dispatcher's as that path does, `:1650-1654`). Code lines: 2 imports, `templateStaticParams` 3, `atTemplateParams` 13, `invokeArmAtTemplateParams` 15, five edited lines in the type-structure loop, and 5 replacing 2 at the call: 43. Add 1 line for the `-Dprobe.scope` switch and 3 for `skip`. `MieDispatchSub`'s template, stock and shadow, is in `scope/javap-template.txt`. Stock reads `Sub__1()` and calls `loadClosureClass` (`:17`, `:28`). The shadow does `instanceof Sub⟦X⟧` and calls `grab⟦X⟧.the_function` (`:68-72`), then the `Tag` generic's own body, `grab♙⟦X⟧`, as the last arm (`:76`).

|---|---|---|---|
| `MieDispatchSub`: `grab(b)`, `b: Tag[\Blue\] = Mixed` | `ClassCastException`: `Marker⟦Red⟧` is not a `Marker⟦Blue⟧` (`scope/dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:21-22`) | `Marker[Blue]`, and `mb` holds `Marker[Blue]` (`:65-66`) | the same (`:108-109`) |

| `ScopeZZ32Sub`: `grab(t)`, `t: Tag[\ZZ32\] = IntSub`, no multiple instantiation | `ClassCastException`: `IntSub` is not a `Sub⟦fortress\|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32⟧` (`scope/ScopeZZ32Sub.compiled.txt:4-5`) | `SubM[ZZ32]` (`:10`) | not run |
| `ScopeMethod`: `K.grab(b1)`, the same pair as dotted methods | `ClassCastException` (`scope/ScopeMethod.compiled.txt:6-7`) | the same (`:14-15`): not covered | not run |
| `MieDispatch`: `grab(a)`, `a: Any = Both` | `ClassCastException`: `Both` is not a `Tag⟦fortress\|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32⟧` (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:14-15`) | the same (`:58-59`) | `Plain`, the `Any` declaration (`:102`) |
| `MieDispatchAny`: `peek(a1..a3)`, `grab(a1)`, all `Any` | `peek` answers from the value; `grab(a1)`: `Marker⟦Red⟧` is not a `Marker⟦X⟧` (`:27-32`) | the same (`:71-76`) | `Red (the Any declaration)`, five times (`:114-118`) |
| `MieDispatchZZ32`: `peek(a)`, `a: Any = IntTag` | `ClassCastException`, the `ZZ32` spelling (`:37-38`) | the same (`:81-82`) | `other`: the `Any` declaration's string (`:123`) |
| `RouteCProbe` | every call is resolved statically; the same in all three modes (`:42-44`, `:86-88`, `:127-129`) | | |

The last four programs mix a generic and a non-generic declaration of one name, which the specification refuses (§2, §5). `skip` is what the code should do for them if they are not refused.

**What else it changes.**
- The compiler prelude compiled under `callsite` is byte-identical to stock, all five jars (`scope/prelude-compare.txt`).
- The compiler tests that declare a generic overload, or match `overload` or `Generic` in the name, are 43 files (`scope/compiler-tests.txt`). Every run output is identical between stock and `callsite`.
- 34 of them link and run. Their classes are byte-identical in 31. In the other 3, `Compiled12.invariantInference`, `invariantInference2` and `Compiled180`, only the generic dispatcher templates differ. `Compiled180`'s last arm, for example, stops re-reading `T` from the value.
- The other 9 fail identically under both: 8 before a jar is written, `Compiled240` in code generation.
- Under `skip`, 42 outputs are identical. `Compiled12.invariantInference` changes: its twelve calls pass `Any`-typed arguments to `f(x: Any, z: Any, y: Any)` beside six generics, and all twelve now print `Any`. Its `.test` expects the run-time answers, so that gated test would go red. The sentence refuses the same file at compile time (§5).

**The remainder**, not built, by site:
- Generic dotted methods. Their dispatcher template comes from `OverloadSet.java:2296-2340` (`generateGenericFunctionClass` with `generateBody(mv, 1)`), with the trait's parameters ahead of the method's (`:2315-2316`). The arms are invoked at `:2240-2265` and the tables named at `:2386-2410`. `ScopeMethod` fails identically, stock and shadow.
- Functional methods in a top-level set. Their static parameters are the trait's plus their own (`:1881-1890`); the shadow guards them out.
- Non-type static parameters. An `opr` parameter has its own naming (`Naming.oprArgAnnotatedRTTI`), and a `nat` parameter needs the size work's run-time kind (FACTS, design A). The shadow guards them out with `KindType`.
- An arm whose static-parameter count differs from its dispatcher's stays on the value path. `Compiled12.invariantInference`'s `[\X1, X extends X1\]` beside `[\X\]` is one; the sentence refuses it.
- A non-generic dispatcher with generic arms stays on the value path unless `skip` is used. The sentence makes it impossible.
- Once the sentence holds and methods are converted, the value-inference block (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`) and `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass` (`:160-213`) are dead code.

## 4. The two side defects

**A generic reached through a less specific declaration throws when its return type mentions the parameter.** The value-reading arm ends with a cast to the arm's declared return type, spelled with the arm's own parameter names (`OverloadSet.java:1720-1727`). In a dispatcher that is not a template, nothing rewrites `X`, so the cast is to the template class `Marker⟦X⟧` itself. `MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a1)` throws this way under stock and `callsite` alike (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:31-32`, `:75-76`). The same cast also goes wrong inside a template whenever the arm names its parameters differently from the dispatcher: the loader rewrites only the dispatcher's names. Stock `ScopeArms` casts to an unrewritten `Marker⟦Y⟧` (`ScopeArms.compiled.txt:5-6`). Stock `ScopeAlpha2` gets its `Marker⟦B,A⟧` rewritten with the dispatcher's map to `Marker⟦Blue,Red⟧` (`ScopeAlpha2.compiled.txt:5`). No multiple instantiation is involved in either. **The change fixes it inside templates**: a renamed arm takes the no-inference path, whose call returns the right type without that cast, and both probes pass. It leaves the defect in non-template dispatchers (`MieDispatchAny` under `callsite`) and in dotted methods. `skip` removes that path, and the sentence makes it unreachable for top-level functions, because a set that mixes generic and non-generic declarations is refused.

**A `ZZ32` instantiation made at run time is spelled differently from the static one.** `loadClosureClass` spells each argument with `RTTI.className()`, the RTTI's own Java class: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32` becomes `fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32` (`RTHelpers.java:174-175`, `RTTI.java:53-58`). Static code spells `ZZ32` as `com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32` (`javap-excerpts.txt:6`). The dispatcher's value path is its only caller (`OverloadSet.java:1696`). `ScopeZZ32Sub` reaches it through a template with no multiple instantiation. Stock throws: `IntSub` is not a `Sub⟦fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32⟧` (`ScopeZZ32Sub.compiled.txt:5`). Under `callsite` the arm is named `grab⟦X⟧` inside the template, the loader writes the call site's own spelling, and it prints `SubM[ZZ32]` (`:10`). **The change avoids the defect on the template path and does not remove it.** `MieDispatchZZ32` and `MieDispatch`'s `grab(a)` still throw under `callsite` (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:81-82`, `:58-59`), and `skip` removes that path. The two spellings remain: the generated RTTI factories also build class names from `RTTI.className()` (`RTHelpers.getRTTIclass`, `:18-54`, called from `InstantiatingClassloader.java:2810`), untouched and unmeasured here.

## 5. What the specification's overload sentence refuses, measured

**The check.** It is in `checkOverloading`'s pair loop (`OverloadingChecker.scala:383`, before the existing rules; `scope-shadow.patch`, second file, 19 code lines). Two declarations of one name are refused when their static parameters differ in number, in kind, or in bounds after positional renaming. "Static parameters" has two readings for a functional method. Under `own` it is only the method's own list. Under `lifted` the trait's parameters come first, which is how the checker already builds its arrows for a top-level set (`STypesUtil.scala:123-127`). Like every rule of this checker, the check never sees a symbolic operator (`OverloadingChecker.scala:546-550`), and in a component it sees only declarations with a body (`:117-121`). The text scan `sentence-scan.py` counts both apart. On the two library apis it agrees with the checker exactly under `own` (179 of 179, none extra) and finds 326 of 335 under `lifted`.

**The interpreter's library.** `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `RangeInternals.fsi` were checked through the zero probe's stack (`scope/sentence-library.txt`). The stack needed three adjustments for the current tree. Its memo hunks are dropped, since the tree has had its own memo since `d28cf74d0`. Its five api edits give way to the tree's own repair of the same defects (`a7ced6764`). `QQ`'s `comprises { AnyIntegral, ... }` is written as the zero stack had it, because the tree's form stops the api's check with an earlier error. The stock run gives 203 errors, the triage's figure (`sentence-library.txt:4`).

| reading | pairs refused | of them the stock rules already refuse | whole-unit errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own` | 179 | 11 | 382 |
| `lifted` | 335 | 43 | 538 |

- The 43 are the triage's 35 plus the 8 it said the sentence also reaches (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md:52-59`). The other pairs are ones the stock rules accept.
- The 156 pairs found only under `lifted` are all a functional method of a generic trait beside one of the same name in another trait or object, most often its own implementation. Examples are `Integral[\I\]`'s twelve operators (`GCD`, `LCM`, `REM`, `MOD`, `DIV`, `CHOOSE`, four bit and two shift operators; 36 pairs) beside `ZZ32`'s, `ZZ64`'s and `NN64`'s. The `lifted` reading therefore refuses implementing a generic trait's functional method in a non-generic subtype, which the tower cannot survive. The triage families `CAP` (20), `seq` (6) and `MINMAX` (5) appear only under this reading.
- Symbolic operators add 329 pairs under `own` by the text scan (`sentence-corpora.txt`): `-` 116, `+` 53, `=` 47, `<` 25, `:` 25, `#` 25, `>=` 13, `>` 9, `<=` 9, `::` 6, and one `BIG //`. They are the same shapes.

The families under `own`, each with the rewrite that satisfies the sentence and what the interpreter does with it:
- **juxtaposition 80, DOT 48**: the tower's functional methods, which have no static parameters (`.fsi:271-520`, `:2360-2362`), beside the vector and matrix products. The api already pads every product to one list, `[\T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\]` (`.fsi:1512-1647`); the component declares one to three (`.fss:2265-2642`). The only rewrites are padding the scalar side to the same four parameters or using another operator for one side. The interpreter loads the padded api today.
- **CMP 25**: comparison and tower methods (none) beside the tuple orders `CMP[\A,B\]` and `CMP[\A,B,C\]` (`.fsi:2495`, `:2501`). Rename the tuple orders, which the interpreter accepts.
- **MIN 8, MAX 8**: `StandardMin`/`Max`/`MinMax`, `Number` and `QQ` (none) beside the array-scalar block `[\T extends Number, I\]` (`.fsi:2556-2559`). Rename the array forms, which the interpreter accepts.
- **openRangeHelper 3, SCMP 3, PCMP 3**: one, two and three parameters for one to three dimensions (`RangeInternals.fsi:612-616`, `:30-40`). Pad each to three parameters, or rename by arity. The interpreter accepts padding (`ScopePad`, `walk.txt`).
- **__cond 1**: `[\E,R\]` and `[\E\]` (`.fsi:755-756`), the generator `if` with and without `else`, a name the desugarer emits (`WellKnownNames.java:65`). Pad the second with `R`; the interpreter accepts padding.

`ScopePad` is the padding repair in small: `pad[\A,B\](x: Box[\A\])` beside `pad[\A,B\](x: Box[\A\], y: Box[\B\])`. It passes the check and prints `one`/`two` compiled (`ScopePad.compiled.txt`) and under `walk`.

**The rest of the library and the builtins.** The compiler prelude compiled with the check on is refused nothing under either reading: `AnyType`, `CompilerBuiltin` and the three `Compiler*` libraries (`sentence-corpora.txt`). In the zero stack the apis `FortressBuiltin`, `AnyType`, `NatReflect`, `List` and `String` reach the check and are refused nothing (`sentence-library.txt:5-7`). `NativeArray`'s 44 earlier errors stop it before the check; the text scan finds nothing there. The other library files, by the text scan:
- `Generator2.fss:52-57`: `takeleft`, `takeright`;
- `Tuple.fsi:17-24`: `first`, `second`, `third`, one per arity;
- `QuickSort.fsi:16-20`;
- `QuickCheck.fss:728-734`: `__genMatchElse`;
- `Set.fss:76-79`;
- `CovariantCollection.fsi:14-16`: `APPCOV`;
- `Containment` under `lifted` only.

**compiler_tests/** (`sentence-corpora.txt`). The checker was run on 48 candidates: the 43 of §3, the text scan's hits under either reading, and every program declaring a name the prelude declares. It refuses 6 programs, the same 6 under both readings, and all are gated:
- `Compiled12.invariantInference` (14 pairs) and `invariantInference2` (8), both through `Compiled12.invariantInference.test`;
- `Compiled14`: `f[\T\]()` beside `f[\T extends ZZ32\](x: T)`, through `Compiled14.test`;
- `Compiled16f`: `g(x: String)` beside the functional method `g[\S extends ZZ32, U\](self)`, through `Compiled16.test`;
- `Compiled10.Comprehensions3`: two `__generate`, through `AfterTypeChecking.test`'s `typecheck`;
- `Compiled6.ak`: `XXX6ak.test` expects exactly two errors, and the check adds a third.

The judge named two of the six. `Comprehensions4` and `Compiled18` have earlier errors and never reach the check. A full sweep, stopped for time after the first 95 programs in name order, refused only `Comprehensions3` among them.

**tests/ and library_tests/**, by the text scan only. The checker cannot take them one at a time: the zero stack re-checks the whole library first, three minutes a run. Under `own`, 9 programs in `tests/` are hit:
- 6 are gated: `overloadTest8.fss:33-37`, `doubledOverloading.fss:36-41`, `GeneratorNullPointer.fss:18-20`, `ArrayListQuick.fss:36-55`, `PureListQuick.fss:36-55`, and `genericMethod4.fss:21-22`, whose dotted `g[\T\](t:T)` sits beside `g[\T, V\](t1:T, t2:T)` and which a column-0 grep cannot see;
- 3 are expected failures: `XXXgenericMethod1` to `3`.

`lifted` adds `fmTest3`. `library_tests/` has none.

## 6. Not settled

- **The specification is not uniform on when static arguments are fixed.** `overloading.tex:136-138` fixes them before applicability. `:173-175`, read alone, says of any "call f(C)", dynamic calls included (`:135-136`): "If the parameter type P includes static parameters, they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference} before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call". That is the interpreter's model. The chapter it cites is empty: "This chapter will include the Fortress static type inference mechanism." (`inference.tex:15`).
- **Which static parameters a functional method has.** The specification does not say. `lifted` refuses implementations of a generic trait's functional methods, and `own` does not; this note recommends neither.
- **Whether the sentence covers operators and different arities.** It says "multiple declarations with the same functional name" (`:100-101`), and operators overload by name like functions ("Operator declarations with the same name but different fixity are not a valid overloading", `:87-88`). Taken literally it refuses scalar `juxtaposition` beside matrix `juxtaposition` unless the scalar side is padded, and `genericMethod4`'s one- and two-argument `g`.
- **The interpreter, measured in passing** (`walk.txt`). Its overload check depends on names: `ScopeArms` (`Y`) and `ScopeAlpha2` are refused at load, while `ScopeArmsX` (both `X`) and `MieDispatchSub` load. On `ScopeArmsX` it answers `TagM[Blue]` for `grab(r)` with `r: Sub[\Red\]`, a value outside the call's static type `Marker[\Red\]`; the compiled path gives `SubM[Red]`. `MieDispatchSub`'s `grab(r)` gives `Marker[Blue]` there.
- **Not built:** generic dotted methods, functional methods, `opr` and `nat` parameters (§3). Their size is unmeasured.
- **Not run:** the gate. The shadow's effect on `ant testFast` is not known beyond the 43 programs of §3.
- **The text scan is not the checker** for `tests/`, `library_tests/` and the library components. In a component it also counts abstract declarations, which the checker leaves out.

<!-- Written 2026-09-23 by a delegated worker for Pavol's choice between the two routes on the compiled checker's multiple instantiation exclusion. This note prices route A of ../multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md § 8, "keep the rule"; the sibling note scope-call-site-dispatch.md prices "drop the rule". Measured on main a0617d672, JDK 25, FORTRESS_THREADS=1. Nothing tracked was modified. The interpreter probes ran under walk with private caches. The run-time survey is a classpath shadow of eight interpreter sources, made by keep/nestprobe/make-shadow.py and put ahead of ProjectFortress/build. The checker count is the gate's own driver run on library copies made by keep/make-flat-lib.py. Commands and captures are in keep/. -->

# The price of keeping the rule: the tower flattened, what depends on the nesting, what the interpreter needs

Terms.
- **Nested tower**: today's library. `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number`, and each level carries the self-typed algebra traits at its own type.
- **Flat tower**: the compiler prelude's shape. The numeric types are siblings under a `Number` without algebra, and widening is a `coerce` declaration.
- **Leaf**: the tower type an object belongs to directly: `Int` and `IntLiteral` → `ZZ32`, `Long` → `ZZ64`, `BigNum` → `ZZ`, `UnsignedLong` → `NN64`, `Ratio` → `QQ`, `Float` and `FloatLiteral` → `RR64`.
- **Dependent site**: a place in a program where a type check passes only because of the nesting.

**The short answer.**
- **The flat tower is 14 declaration headers** in the library's four core files (§ 1). The 10 objects that only inherit an instantiation keep their text. The algebra moves to the leaves, widening becomes `coerce`, and `Number`'s catch-alls go.
- **The nesting carries weight under walk.** A run-time survey over the 392 test files finds 235 dependent sites in 19 library files and 994 in the text of 75 test files (§ 2).
  - 160 of the library sites and 207 of the test sites certainly need a conversion.
  - 15 inherited methods need restating on the leaves.
  - One library line, `FortressLibrary.fss:4121`, is reached by every test expected to pass.
- **The interpreter has no coercion, but its phase order already turns every `coerce` into a callable `coerce_<trait>`** (§ 3). Calling them at dispatch and at typed bindings is about 150-200 lines in six files. It would resolve coercions at run time, where the specification resolves them statically.
- **Converting by hand instead** means the sites counted above, and the same again in every new program.
- **The compiled side's own tests widen by coercion, never by hand.**
- **The flat tower takes the checker count from 103 to 22** (§ 5): all 61 exclusion errors go. The count is still masked by `FortressLibrary.fsi:2526`, and it does not reach the library's bodies.

## 1. What "flat" means for this library

The rule only bites where a type adds its own instantiation of a self-typed trait below a type that already has one. `ZZ32 extends ZZ64` is refused because `ZZ32` adds `Integral[\ZZ32\]` beside `ZZ64`'s `Integral[\ZZ64\]`. An object that adds nothing is legal under the rule: `Int extends ZZ32`, `Long`, `UnsignedLong`, `IntLiteral`, `BigNum`, and also `RR32 extends RR64`. So 14 declaration headers change. 12 of them are among the review's 23 declarations with errors (§ 5 there): all but the 10 objects and `Maybe`, whose errors go with `AnyMaybe`'s fix. The other two are `Number` and `RR64`, which have no errors but must take or give up the algebra. The 10 objects and `Maybe` keep their text. The rewrite is `keep/flat-tower-sketch.fsi`, and `keep/make-flat-lib.py` applies exactly those headers to copies.
- **The `extends` clauses that go**: `Number extends` its four self-typed traits, `QQ extends RR64`, `AnyIntegral extends QQ`, `ZZ64 extends ZZ`, `NN64 extends ZZ`, `ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, `NN32 extends NN64`, and `Integral[\I\] extends AnyIntegral`. Also `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]` on `TotalComparison` (the prelude's own edit, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:1521-1523`), `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` on `AnyMaybe`, and the five `DistributesOver` markers on `SumReduction` and `ProdReduction`.
- **The `excludes` clauses that come**: each integer leaf excludes its integer siblings. `RR64` and `QQ` exclude each other and `AnyIntegral`, as the prelude's `ZZ32 … excludes { ZZ64, RR32, RR64 }` does (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`).
- **Where the algebra sits**: on the leaves only, as in the prelude. Each integer leaf extends `AnyIntegral` and `Integral[\Self\]`. `Integral[\I\]` extends `StandardTotalOrder[\I\]` and `AdditiveGroup[\I\]`, no longer `AnyIntegral`. `RR64` and `QQ` extend `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardMinMax`, `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, each at their own type. `Number` keeps only the two markers, `AnyAdditiveGroup` and `AnyMultiplicativeRing`. They carry no methods, so the arrays' `excludes AnyMultiplicativeRing` stays true of every number (`FortressLibrary.fss:2195`, `:2503`, `:2670`).
- **Why not on `Number` only**: an integer that extends `Integral[\ZZ32\]` gets `Equality[\ZZ32\]` through `StandardTotalOrder`, beside `Number`'s `Equality[\Number\]`. So under "Number only", no integer could be `Integral`. The ranges' bound `I extends Integral[\I\]` (92 lines of `RangeInternals.fsi`) would then admit nothing.
- **What `Number` loses**: its operator and function declarations, 52 in the api and 57 in the component, the catch-alls such as `opr +(self, b:Number): RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` (`FortressLibrary.fss:379`). Two reasons, both from the prelude's choice:
  - A catch-all applies without coercion to every mixed call. The specification tries coercion only when no declaration applies without it (`conversions-coercions.tex:454-458`), so `x + 1` with `x: ZZ64` would go to float arithmetic, not to `ZZ64`'s `+`.
  - The catch-all returns `RR64`. Once `ZZ32` is not below `RR64`, that result breaks the return type rule against each leaf's own `+`.
- **Widening**: `coerce` on the wider type. `ZZ64` takes a `ZZ32`; `ZZ` takes the four fixed widths; `NN64` takes an `NN32`. `QQ` and `RR64` take the five integer leaves, and `RR64` also takes a `QQ`. The prelude has the first three groups (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:514-518`, `:575-576`, `:816-817`). It has no coercion from an integer into a float.
- **`comprises` clauses**: each leaf comprises its own objects only (`QQ`'s component clause becomes `{ Ratio }`, and the api keeps `{ ... }`), and `Number` has none, as in the prelude. `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ, ZZ64, ZZ32, NN64, NN32 }` becomes well formed, because the five leaves now extend it directly. With it go the family E error at `FortressLibrary.fsi:409-411`, its `NOT YET` comment, and the five-line `isEligibleToExtend` accommodation approved on 2026-09-21 (`POSITIONS.md:48`).
- **Methods a leaf inherits today** have to be restated on the leaf, or once on `Integral[\I\]`. The survey of § 2 finds 15 such method names that the tests use.

## 2. What depends on the nesting, measured

Method. A text grep gives candidates. A run-time survey then gives the dependent sites. The survey is `keep/nestprobe/NestProbe.java`, with hooks in `FType.typeMatch` (parameters, typed bindings), `LHSEvaluator` (typed local declarations), `Evaluator.forTypecase`, and `MethodClosure.applyMethod` (the trait that defined the body that runs). It records every check that passes only through the nesting, with its call site, and it changes no behaviour. All 392 `.fss` files in `ProjectFortress/tests/` ran under it (`keep/nestprobe/run-tests.sh`).

The survey counts a site once, whatever the number of tests that reach it. It splits the sites by what the flat library would need there:
- **A conversion at the site**: a value reaches a declared type above its leaf; or a mixed call is answered by a wider leaf's method (`ZZ64`'s `+` with an `Int` as `self`); or one of `Number`'s catch-alls runs.
- **Only a method restated on the leaf**: the leaf lacks a method it inherits today, such as `QQ`'s `=/=` for an `Int`. The parameter check of that same inherited method at that site counts here too, because the restated method takes the leaf's own type.

Captures: `keep/nestprobe/survey-summary.txt`, and one row per site in `survey-sites.tsv`.

**(a) The library.**
- **Text candidates**: 212 lines outside the tower's own declarations name `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64`, `NN64` or `AnyIntegral`, in 16 library files. 36 of them are in `FortressLibrary.fss`. `FortressBuiltin.fss` has none outside its numeric objects.
- **What the tests execute**: 235 dependent sites in 19 library files, none in `FortressBuiltin.fss`.
  - **190 need a conversion.** 160 certainly: 44 in `FortressLibrary.fss` and 116 in the other files. 30 more if the float operand's partner is an integer; these are `Number`'s catch-alls on floats, which run today for a `Float` with a `FloatLiteral`, and `RR64`'s own arithmetic fixes that case in the library.
  - **45 need only a restated method.**
- **`Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, 90 sites, by line**: `35` (`cast[\T\]`'s `typecase` at `T = ZZ`), `52` (`COMPOSE`), `297` (`assert(x, y)`'s `x =/= y`, reached by 78 tests), `367`, `451`, `461` (`Number`'s and `RR64`'s own bodies calling `Number`'s comparisons on floats), `475-521` (`simplestRationalBetween`), `532-596` (`QQ`'s bodies), `607` (`Ratio.asFloat`), `632` (`Integral.DIVIDES`), `710-720` (`ZZ64`), `838-894` (`ZZ`);
  `1336`, `1750`, `1827-1994` (array bodies given an integer where a float element is declared), `2197-2278` (`Vector`), `2505-2570` (`Matrix`), `3040` (`SumReduction.join`), `4121` (`__globalTimeInformation: ZZ64 := 0`), `4509-4519` (the scalar-extension block).
- **The other library files, 145 sites**: `Map` 32, `IntMap` 19, `Set` 18, `Format` 18, `Random` 14, `QuickCheck` 12, `Sparse` 8, `Timing` 6, `RangeInternals` 4, `List` 4, `ChunkedSparseArray` 3, and one each in seven more. Six further sites are in `test_library/ArrayOperatorVocabulary.fss` and in interpreter-generated code.
- **The methods to restate** are 24 (method, leaf) pairs over 15 names (`survey-methods.tsv`): from `QQ`, `/`, `=/=`, `floor`, `ceiling`, `truncate`, `MINNUM` and `MAXNUM`; from `ZZ`, `/`, `numerator`, `odd`, `even`, `cmp` and `widen`; from `ZZ64`, `narrow` and `big`; and `SQRT` on `RR64`.

**(b) The tests.**
- **By grep**: 49 of the 392 `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` name a type above `ZZ32`, or mix an integer and a float literal in one arithmetic expression. 47 name such a type and 8 bind an integer literal to one.
- **By the survey**: 994 dependent sites in the text of 75 test files.
  - **336 need a conversion**, in 49 files. 207 of them certainly, in 35 files. The rest are the float catch-alls above.
  - **658 need only a restated method.** 599 of them are `RationalTest.fss`'s integer `/`; that file has 703 sites in all.
  - **Sampled to confirm** (`survey-sites.tsv`): `3 + 5 / 4` (`DivPrecedence.fss:18`), `1+BITNOT xfoo` with `xfoo: ZZ` (`UnsignedTest.fss:51`), `(1 + SQRT 5) / 2` (`fib13.fss:15`), and `fib13[\ZZ64\](20)` binding the literal to a `ZZ64` (`:28`).
- **What a run reaches**: every test expected to pass reaches `FortressLibrary.fss:4121`: 357 of the 392 runs. The 35 that do not are all `XXX` expected-failure tests. So one library line stops the whole suite until it is converted. Beyond that line, 143 tests reach a dependent site, and 109 reach one that certainly needs a conversion.
- **`library_tests/`**: 12 of its 40 `.fss` name a type above `ZZ32`, and 9 bind an integer literal to one. They are compiled-path tests, and they rely on coercion (§ 3).

**(c) The "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically" and the `DistributesOver` markers.**
- **The hack**: `SumReduction.join(a: Number, b: Number): Number = a+b` and `empty(): Number = 0` (`FortressLibrary.fss:3039-3040`, and `ProdReduction` at `:3062-3063`) work only through `Number`'s catch-all `+` and the nesting. The survey sees `:3040` run it for `RR64` and `ZZ32` values. The flat `Number` has no `+`, so the compiled checker cannot type `a+b` on `Number`, and three replacements are open:
  - a parametric reduction lifted to `Maybe`, as `MinReduction[\T extends StandardMin[\T\]\]` already is (`:3115`). A sum over an empty generator then has no identity: today it is `0`.
  - One reduction per leaf, eight of them, picked by a `SUM` overload per element type.
  - The identity passed in by the caller.

  The prelude has no `SUM`, so it gives no precedent.
- **The `DistributesOver` markers are read nowhere.** Their only reader is commented out (`Generator2.fss:59-70`). Distributivity is decided by the `distribute(r)` methods (`FortressLibrary.fss:3041-3048`, `:3064-3065`) through `distributes(q, r)` (`Generator2.fss:73`). So they go, and nothing replaces them. A marker wanted later would be one non-generic trait per fact, the library's own `AnyMultiplicativeRing` pattern.

## 3. What the interpreter needs

The probes use a flat two-level tower in the prelude's shape: `trait Wide extends { Num, Equality[\Wide\] } excludes { Narrow }` with `coerce(x: Narrow)`, beside `Narrow`. Under walk, a `Narrow` fails at each of the three kinds of check:
- `f(x: Wide)`, not overloaded: "Unification error: Closure/Constructor for f param 1 (x:Wide) got arg NarrowOf" (`keep/FlatCall.walk.txt:4-5`).
- `g(Wide)` beside `g(String)`: "Failed to find any matching overload, args = (NarrowOf)" (`keep/FlatOverload.walk.txt:5`).
- `w: Wide = NarrowOf(3)`: "RHS expression type NarrowOf is not assignable to LHS type Wide" (`keep/FlatBind.walk.txt:4`).

The library's own nesting takes the same calls today: `h(3)` for `h(x: ZZ64)`, `k(3)` for `k(x: RR64)` and `q: QQ = z` all run (`keep/FlatExplicit.walk.txt:3-5`).

**Remedy (i), coercion in the interpreter.** The coercions are already there to be called. The interpreter's phase order runs the disambiguator's `CoercionLifter` (`compiler/Disambiguator.java:287-288`), which turns each trait's `coerce` into a top-level function `coerce_<trait>` (`NamingCzar.java:106`, `:1708-1710`). `FlatLifted` calls `coerce_Wide(n)` by hand under walk, and the call works (`keep/FlatLifted.walk.txt:2`). What is missing is the decision to call them:
- `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:787-801`), where the team left "TODO add checks for COERCE, right here." (`:791`). It needs a second pass when no overload applies: the overloads applicable with coercion, the most specific one (`conversions-coercions.tex:515-535`), and the plan kept in the per-argument-type cache (`:760-776`). Overloaded methods go through the same function (`OverloadedMethod.java:50`). About 80 lines.
- A single closure: `NonPrimitive.buildEnvFromParams` (`NonPrimitive.java:242-255`) and `typecheckParams` (`:147`, `:164`).
- The typed bindings: `LHSEvaluator.java:97` and `:215`, `BuildEnvironments.java:224`, `:753` and `:774`, and `BaseEnv.java:314`. With the three `NonPrimitive` sites, that is nine sites at about 5 lines each. The specification's third context, a declared return type (`conversions-coercions.tex:98-110`), would be a new check: the interpreter records it (`FunctionClosure.java:41`) but never tests a result against it.
- A helper that finds `coerce_<T>` in the environment where `T` is declared, tests it and applies it: about 40 lines. `FType.typeMatch` (`FType.java:108-113`) is the one test all these sites share. In total, about 150-200 lines of Java in six files (seven with the return check), plus tests.
- Not covered: generic inference (`EvaluatorBase.inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). With mixed widths it infers a join, and the join of `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` in a flat tower is `AnyIntegral`, for example in `lo:hi`. What the interpreter then does with that join is not measured.
- The semantics would differ from the specification's. It resolves coercion statically: "Notice that coercion is resolved statically. … the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time" (`conversions-coercions.tex:567-570`). Its own example has `c: C = D` and `f(c)`, where `D` is both a `B` and a `C`. The call "resolves to the declaration f(A) despite the fact that the declaration f(B) is applicable to the dynamic call f(D) and does not require coercion" (`:572-604`). An interpreter that coerces at run time would call `f(B)`. The compiled path would follow the specification, and the two paths would answer differently.

**Remedy (ii), explicit widening at each dependent site**:
- `survey-summary.txt` counts the sites. They are 160 certain library sites and 207 in the tests, in 35 test files, plus up to 159 float catch-all sites (30 in the library, 129 in the tests) where the partner is an integer. With them come the 15 methods restated on the leaves, which are library work under either remedy.
- **Each literal bound to a wider type needs a spelling**: `widen(0)` for `ZZ64`, `big(0)` for `ZZ`, `0.0` for `RR64`. The interpreter makes every literal within `ZZ32`'s range an `Int` (`FIntLiteral.make`, `FIntLiteral.java:40-56`). It has no way to write a small literal of another width.
- **Mixed widths need a `widen` or `asFloat` at the call.**
- **The cost is paid again in every future program.** That includes the ones the one library exists to serve: microGPT's `(step 1.0) / (numSteps 1.0)` (`explorations/microgpt.fss:243`).

**The compiled side's precedent is coercion, never widening by hand.** `library_tests/Integer.test` compiles and runs `Integer1-4`, `IntegerChoose1-2`, `ShiftTest`, `ShiftTest2` and `AverageTest` against the prelude. They write `three: ZZ64 = 3` (`Integer2.fss:18`). They pass `i`, a `ZZ32` from `0:7`, to `testLongAverage(x: ZZ64, y: ZZ64)` (`AverageTest.fss:108`). They compute `longSeed BOXCROSS intMult` (`ZZ64` by `ZZ32`, `:128`) and `unsignedLongSeed BOXCROSS unsignedIntMult` (`NN64` by `NN32`, `:138`). Every one of these goes through the prelude's `coerce` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:575-576`, `:816-817`, and the `IntLiteral` ones). Of the 40 `.fss` in `library_tests/`, 12 name a type wider than `ZZ32`, and 9 bind an integer literal to one. None converts by hand.

## 4. What the flat shape forecloses or changes

- **The specification's `Empty extends List[\T\]`** (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:384-397`). Keeping the rule refuses it on the compiled path, whatever the tower looks like; the flat tower neither helps nor hurts it. Under walk it stays accepted (`MieDecl.walk.txt`).
- **The specification's promotion story.** The mathematical sets nest by subtyping: "ℤ (ZZ) is the set of integers (it is a subtype of ℚ and ℤ*)" (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:28-29`), and ℚ "is a subtype of ℝ and ℚ*" (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:36-37`). Between machine types, widening is coercion:
  - "it is convenient to be able to use an integer-valued expression in a floating-point expression even though its type is not a subtype of any floating-point type. Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values (the technical term for this kind of automatic conversion is coercion)" (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:61-66`).
  - The only example with `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` declares `trait ZZ32 end` and `trait ZZ64 coerce(z: ZZ32) = … end`: "the call f(ZZ32) resolves to the declaration f(ZZ64) because ZZ64 ≺ ZZ128, which follows from the fact that ZZ64 coerces to ZZ128" (`:549-565`).
  - The libraries "define coercions from numerals to integers (for simple numerals) and rational numbers (for compound numerals)" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex:146-148`). The chapter's own note says "Widening and where clauses are not yet supported." (`:15`).
  - No sentence in `Specification/` makes `ZZ32` a subtype of `ZZ64`, or `QQ` a subtype of `RR64`: a grep of every `.tex` finds the fixed widths only in that example and in examples of other things. So for those two links the flat shape's mechanism is the specification's own. What the flat shape loses against the specification is `ZZ <: QQ`. Both carry `StandardPartialOrder` at their own type, which is Naden's open case: "more work needs to be done in order to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:631-632`).
- **`Number` bounds in C4 and the array vocabulary** (`FACTS.md:94`). `T extends Number` stays valid, because every leaf is still a `Number`. Two things change:
  - **Arithmetic between leaves needs a coercion or a conversion.** The scalar-extension block and the `Vector` and `Matrix` bodies are among § 2's library sites; at `FortressLibrary.fss:2212` and `:2570`, an `Int` reaches a declared `RR64` element.
  - **One gain:** `RR64` extends `AdditiveGroup[\RR64\]`, so the specification's bound `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, which the shipped `RR64` fails (`FACTS.md:98`), becomes usable.
- **microGPT.** The survey on `explorations/microgpt.fss` ran 50 of its 250 training steps and found 37 dependent sites in its text (`keep/nestprobe/showcase-microgpt-sites.tsv`). All 37 go through `Number`'s catch-alls.
  - **7 mix an integer with a float**: the `n 1.0` idiom (`:86`, `:241`, `:243`, `:250-251`), `(… - 48) / 100.0` (`:63`), and `SQRT(hd 1.0)` (`:208`). They need a coercion from the integer, or `asFloat`.
  - **30 are floats only.** `var grad: RR64 := 0.0` (`:17`) stores a `FloatLiteral`, and adding it to a `Float` goes through `Number`'s `+`: 941K calls at `:50` alone. `RR64`'s own arithmetic in the library fixes these 30.
- **Row 330** (`POSITIONS.md:49`: "ℤ sits under ℚ under ℝ64 in the tower, so an integer result goes back into float arithmetic by promotion"). In the flat shape `ZZ` is under neither, so there is no promotion by subtyping.
  - The promotion survives only as the sketch's `RR64` `coerce(x: ZZ)`. The prelude does not have that coercion today.
  - On the compiled path it is static: in `floor(x) + y` with `y: RR64`, no `+` applies without coercion, and `RR64`'s applies once `floor(x)` is coerced.
  - Under walk the promotion needs remedy (i). With remedy (ii) the program writes `asFloat(floor(x))`.
  - Whether the compiled checker coerces a functional method's `self` position is not measured.
  - The other half of the reasoning is untouched: `ZZ` is unbounded and cannot overflow.

## 5. The checker count under the flat shape, measured

`keep/count-variant.sh` runs the gate's own driver, checker shadow and table (`coordinator/tools/checker-count/`) on library copies whose directory shadows the tree's `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin` (`Shell.sourcePath`, `Shell.java:1175-1188`). Each copy has a fresh private cache. `keep/count-diff.py` compares the errors one by one, setting aside the copy's shifted line numbers (`keep/count/`).
- **The unchanged copy: 103**, the gate's table (`table-L0.txt`).
- **The flat copy: 22** (`table-FLAT.txt`, `diff-L0-FLAT.txt`).
  - **82 go**: all 61 hierarchy errors that `checkP` caused (35 family A, 26 family B); both family E comprises errors (`.fsi:409`, `:411`); and 19 overloading errors in `RangeInternals.fsi` (7 `combine2D`, 7 `combine3D` and 5 `CAP` pairs), by a mechanism not traced.
  - **1 appears**: `IN` at `RangeInternals.fsi:429` against `:505`, also not traced.
  - **21 stay**: 17 overloading errors in `RangeInternals.fsi`, 3 return-type errors (`:257`, `:259`, `:319` against `BoundedRange`), and the family A error at `FortressLibrary.fsi:2526` (`excludes Condition[\()\]`).
- **The flat copy that keeps `Number`'s 52 declarations also gives 22** (`table-FLATN.txt`). The `FortressLibrary` api still stops at its hierarchy stage on `:2526`, so its overloading check never examines them.
- **The 22 is masked, as the 103 is.**
  - Repairing `:2526` took that api from 2 errors to 260 in the zero probe (`perf-probes/nat/zero.md` § 3).
  - The component is never type-checked, so none of § 2's sites is counted.
  - `NativeArray` still crashes the overloading checker.
- **For comparison**, relaxing `checkP` gave 93 → 33 on the older tree (`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md` § 5). `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` prices the other route on this tree.

## 6. The size, and what is not settled

- **The library rewrite** has five parts:
  - **The 14 headers**: 58 changed lines in `FortressLibrary.fsi` and 62 in `FortressLibrary.fss` (the `FLATN` copy), plus one line in each `FortressBuiltin` file.
  - **What `Number` gives up and `RR64` takes on**: `Number`'s 52 api declarations and 57 bodies go; `RR64` gets its own arithmetic and the float functions. That is what a `Float` meeting a `FloatLiteral` uses today, including microGPT's 30 float-only sites.
  - **The 15 restated methods**, most once on `Integral[\I\]`.
  - **Smaller pieces**: `ZZ`'s `/` returning `Ratio(a, 1)`, and `TotalComparison`'s inherited `MIN`, `MAX`, `<=` and `>=` written by hand.
  - **A new `SUM` and `PROD`** (§ 2c).
- **The interpreter remedy this price assumes is (i), coercion**: about 150-200 lines in six files, plus tests. It is the compiled side's own mechanism, and it keeps today's programs as written. Remedy (ii) would edit 160 library sites and 207 test sites in 35 files now, plus up to 159 float sites, and it would do the same to every new program. The price of (i) is § 3's divergence: coercion chosen at run time, where the specification and the compiled path choose it statically.
- **The tests that change**:
  - **Under (i), no test text by design, but some results can change.** In the nested tower a declared wider type converts nothing. `x: ZZ64 = 2147483647` holds an `Int`, and `x + 1` prints `-2147483648` (`keep/NestedWidth.walk.txt:2-3`). A coercion makes it a `Long`. How many tests print such a result was not measured. One site needs a conversion regardless: the `typecase` at `FortressLibrary.fss:35`, because `typecase` is not among the coercion contexts (`conversions-coercions.tex:98-110`).
  - Under (ii), the 35 to 49 test files of § 2.
  - Both need new interpreter tests for coercion, and a compiled test for the integer-to-float coercion.
- **In the project's units**: two rungs, each gated on the full suite (the repair batch's gate run was 739 s, `microgpt-run-c-handover.md`). The interpreter rung for remedy (i) lands first or with the library rung, because the flat library cannot pass the gate without it: `FortressLibrary.fss:4121` alone stops every test. The checker needs no change, and its count falls to 22.
- **Not settled**:
  - Generic inference over mixed widths, where a flat tower's join is `AnyIntegral` or `Number` (`lo:hi`).
  - Whether the compiled checker coerces a functional method's `self` position.
  - The library code that no test runs: the text grep's 212 candidate lines bound it.
  - The component's type check under the flat tower, which no count reaches yet.
  - The mechanism behind the 19 `RangeInternals` errors that go and the one that appears.
  - Which of the three replacements for the reductions' hack to take.

# What the field did with the exclusion trade after 2012

## 1. The Fortress type group and Karl Naden after 2012

- **POPL 2019 kept the rule for invariant traits and moved the return-type check to run time.** Park, Hong, Steele, Ryu, *Polymorphic symmetric multiple dispatch with variance*, PACMPL 3 (POPL), art. 11, doi:10.1145/3290324 (text from the Wayback copy of the ACM PDF). The core calculus FGFV has multiple inheritance, variance and reified dispatch. Its [Anc-Same-Trait] rule: "if a class C extends two instances of a trait T, T⟦α⟧ and T⟦ρ⟧, then C also extends some T⟦γ⟧ … that extends both … because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait" (p. 11:11). For an invariant T only γ = α = ρ satisfies this (derived here, not stated there), so the invariant case of the exclusion stands, and the covariant case is Naden's "minimal instantiation" refinement.
- Its dispatch uses the call's static return type: "[R-Method] seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" (p. 11:17), because "Supporting variance in a type-sound manner requires keeping track of the static types of method invocations at run time" (p. 11:7). This is the option Naden's write-up describes as "The runtime could be enhanced to include return type constraints when considering applicability" and rejects because "programmers can no longer understand the execution of a program without static type information" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:247-253`, `:288-289`). The paper proves soundness with the ancestor rule in place (sufficiency). It contains no self types and no numeric tower (searched for "self", "comprises", "Integer", "tower"). It leaves out "modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types", which "can be added in an obvious way" (p. 11:25).
- Its precursor is in the tree: `Papers/Welterweight/paper.tick:499-509` (Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, Tristan, "PAPER SUBMITTED TO 2012 ACM SPLASH---OOPSLA"). It states the same rule under the name Ancestors Meet Rule, with the reason: "if an object value belongs to one or more instances of some trait T, there is a *unique minimal instance* of T … being able to identify this minimal instance quickly is essential to the efficient dynamic dispatch algorithms we present later" (`static.tick:83-89`). A self-typed-generics step in its dispatch algorithm is commented out (`dispatch.tick:195-212`).
- **Four Oracle patents, filed 2012-08-31 (the day of Naden's write-up), name inventors from the type group, Naden among them.** US 8,843,887 B2, *Fast dispatch predicate for overloaded functions with generic type hierarchies that lack contravariance* (Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, Luchangco; granted 2014-09-23; https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8843887), and US 8,898,632 B2, *Dispatch predicate … using type intervals* (…/downloadPdf/8898632). Both print the same list of "Restrictions on Fortress types" (8,843,887 col. 7 l. 40 to col. 8 l. 13; 8,898,632 col. 7 l. 52 to col. 8 l. 28). It includes "Minimal instance of generic ancestors: If S<:G[\T\], then there exists U such that for all T where S<:G[\T\]: if G's ith static parameter is invariant, then Ui=Ti", which is the exclusion. It also includes "Self-types meet: if T<:U=S[\U\] and T<:V=S[\V\] then T<:S[\meet(U, V)\] and meet(U, V) must be a declared (not intersection) type. In practice, this means that the instantiations of a particular self-typed generic must form a forest."
- The patents define the idiom: "the 'self-typed generic,' where a generic in T also comprises exactly T … Because the only subtype of Comparable[\T\] is T, the two types include exactly the same sets of values, and are in some sense the same type" (8,843,887 col. 6 l. 40-56). Their inference step lifts a lower bound "to a self-type that simultaneously satisfies the one or more self-typed constraints" (col. 2 l. 35-42; col. 12 l. 1-8). The list does not say how "Self-types meet" combines with the invariant clause. The library's `trait Equality[\T extends Equality[\T\]\]` has no `comprises T` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:72-74`), so it is not a self-typed generic in the patents' sense. This is the only text found that admits the tower's shape, several self-typed instantiations along a chain, inside the rule; no paper published it. Companion patents US 8,893,082 (Naden, Chase, Hilburn: type inference with intervals and inference directions) and US 8,893,098 (deferred type inference) were identified by title only.
- **Naden's TLDI 2012 workshop paper** (*Towards Practical Runtime Type Instantiation*, dated 2011-11-10, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~kbn/pubs/fortressInstantiation.pdf) gives the motivation for specialisation: "designers of the Fortress programming language found it useful while writing their standard library to define both monomorphic and polymorphic versions of functions". Its matching step assumes the exclusion: "we can determine what instantiation Ty′ of Baz is a supertype of Ty (as in [5] we require that this query return the unique minimal answer)", where [5] is Tate et al., PLDI 2011. Applicability there still includes the return bound "[TX/X]τr <: Tr", with Tr "the return type of the statically most specific applicable function signature". Footnote 1 relaxes the scoping rule "in the case of selftypes".
- Naden's later work is on permissions and concurrency: POPL 2012 *A Type System for Borrowing Permissions*, and TOPLAS 36(1) 2014 *Æminium* (Stork, Naden, et al.). Both are listed at https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~aldrich/papers/, which lists no Wyvern paper with him and nothing later. His homepage (© 2011, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~kbn/) says "I am a third year PhD student in the Computer Science Department at Carnegie Mellon University" and "I spent the summer of 2011 as an intern at Oracle Labs East working on the Fortress programming language." Current affiliation: not established. A public org chart lists a "Karl Naden" as Principal Consultant at J2 Interactive (https://theorg.com/org/j2-interactive/org-chart/karl-naden), but no page found names both him and CMU or Fortress, and LinkedIn refused the fetch.
- Other type-group work: Kim and Ryu, CPP 2011 (a Coq model without generics, per POPL 2019 p. 11:4), and Kim, Ryu, Luchangco, Steele, APLAS 2013, doi:10.1007/978-3-319-03542-0_11 (abstract not reachable: the publisher elides it at Semantic Scholar and Springer redirects to login). The Semantic Scholar citation list of the OOPSLA 2011 paper (https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1145/2048066.2048140/citations) has 19 entries. Beyond these three it shows no later paper by Kilpatrick, Hilburn, Allen or Luchangco on the subject.
- **No published resolution of the tower conflict and no proof that the rule is necessary were found.** The published results prove soundness with the rule, and the only necessity argument remains Naden's `BadList` counterexample.

## 2. Julia

- Single abstract inheritance, concrete leaves. "concrete types may not subtype each other: all concrete types are final and may only have abstract types as their supertypes … It turns out that being able to inherit behavior is much more important than being able to inherit structure, and inheriting both causes significant difficulties in traditional object-oriented languages" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/types/, introduction). The tower is `abstract type Real <: Number`, `Integer <: Real`, `Signed <: Integer` and `primitive type Int32 <: Signed 32 end`, `Int64 <: Signed 64` (same page, "Abstract Types", "Primitive Types"). `Int32` is not below `Int64`. Parameters are invariant: "even though Float64 <: Real we DO NOT have Point{Float64} <: Point{Real}".
- The formal account calls it "nominal single subtyping" and says: "There is no notion of soundness in Julia, even for fully type-annotated programs. If a method call does not have a most specific method, a runtime error will be reported. Ambiguity in dispatch is always resolved dynamically." (Zappa Nardelli et al., *Julia subtyping: a rational reconstruction*, OOPSLA 2018, doi:10.1145/3276483, pp. 113:3-4, https://hal.science/hal-01882137/document). The manual's example `g(x::Float64, y)` beside `g(x, y::Float64)` gives "MethodError: g(::Float64, ::Float64) is ambiguous", with the advice "specifying an appropriate method for the intersection case" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/methods/, "Method Ambiguities").
- Follows from those two facts (not stated in a source): each type has one declared supertype and invariant parameters, so a value reaches each parametric ancestor through one chain, and `where T` binds from it. Naden's `BadList` cannot be declared, specialised methods beside generic ones are allowed, and no static return type is promised to break.
- Why no multiple inheritance. Bezanson's thesis (*Abstraction in Technical Computing*, MIT 2015, https://worrydream.com/refs/Bezanson_2015_-_Abstraction_in_Technical_Computing.pdf) lists "Intersections, multiple inheritance" among features that "would be difficult to add, or possibly break decidability of subtyping" (p. 63). Under "Simulating multiple inheritance" it presents Tim Holy's trait-by-dispatch pattern, noting "The original author of a type like Array does not need to know about this property, unlike the situation with multiple inheritance or explicit interfaces" (p. 74, citing github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/2345#issuecomment-54537633). The manual documents it as "Trait-based dispatch" ("Holy-trait" pattern, methods manual).
- Julia issue #5, "abstract multiple inheritance" (Karpinski, 2011-04-27, still open, https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/5), proposed allowing it under one restriction: "If two abstract types are are [sic] used for dispatch in the same 'slot' of the same generic function object then they cannot share a common, concrete descendant". That is an exclusion requirement in the spirit of Fortress's meet rule. It never shipped.
- Mixed arithmetic goes through promotion, not subtyping. `+(x::Number, y::Number) = +(promote(x,y)...)` and "the arguments of functions are never automatically converted"; also "although every Int32 value can also be represented as a Float64 value, Int32 is not a subtype of Float64" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/conversion-and-promotion/; thesis pp. 90-91). On Fortress specifically: its "coerce feature … a built-in notion of type widening … It is not possible to provide these features in Julia without doing violence to our 'everything is a method call' semantics" (thesis p. 94).

## 3. X10

- X10 follows Java's rule: "Limitation: A class or struct may not implement two different instantiations of a generic interface. In particular, a class or struct can implement only one function type." (*X10 Language Specification* v2.6.2, §4.6 Function types, p. 48, Wayback copy of x10.sourceforge.net/documentation/languagespec/x10-262.pdf; the same sentence is in v2.1 of 2011-02-23, p. 50, https://www.classes.cs.uchicago.edu/archive/2011/winter/32102-1/reading/x10-latest.pdf). No reason is given.
- Numbers are structs, which "do not have superclasses, and cannot extend anything" (§4.2.2, p. 33). Mixing goes through implicit widening: "Byte < Short < Int < Long < Float < Double" (§11.23.2, p. 178). Overloads are chosen statically: "Method resolution is the problem of determining, statically, which method … should be invoked" (§8.12, p. 133).
- Its generics are reified (*Fast method dispatch and effective use of primitives for reified generics in managed X10*, X10 Workshop 2012, doi:10.1145/2246056.2246060). The Java back end loses that for one self-typed interface: mapping "x10.lang.Comparable[T] … to java.lang.Comparable … results in the lost of runtime type information for Comparable[T]" (§18.2, p. 244).

## 4. The multiple-dispatch line

- None of the pre-Fortress systems had type parameters. The OOPSLA 2011 paper says of Dubious, MultiJava and F(EML): "None of the systems described above support polymorphic functions or types" (`Papers/Types/related-work.tick:36`). POPL 2019 repeats this (p. 11:25) and adds that ML≤ "lacks multiple inheritance" and that ParaSail "does not support covariant and contravariant type parameters".
- Cecil combined multimethods, multiple inheritance and F-bounded generics by erasing type arguments from dispatch: "Method lookup does not depend on the instantiating types … message sends foo[int]() and foo[string]() will always be dispatched to the same method implementation" (*The Cecil Language: Specification and Rationale*, §4.1.2, http://projectsweb.cs.washington.edu/research/projects/cecil/www/Vortex-Three-One/doc-cecil-lang/cecil-spec-82.html). Its tower puts the self-typed trait at the root only: `extend num isa ordered[num]`, then "num can have subtypes, such as int or float, which can be compared with each other … extend int isa num; extend float isa num; 3 != 3.14 -- legal" (§4.4, …/cecil-spec-86.html). Litvinov's 2003 thesis (ftp.cs.washington.edu) timed out.
- Tate, Leung, Lerner (*Taming Wildcards in Java's Type System*, PLDI 2011, https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~ross/publications/tamewild/tamewild-tate-pldi11.pdf), the source Naden cites for the unique minimal instantiation: "For Java this invocation is always unique, although this is not necessary for our algorithm" (§4.2, p. 5).
- Later work POPL 2019 cites: FHJ (Wang et al. 2018), whose dispatch "uses static types at run time", and Castagna et al. 2015, "a statically-typed calculus with dynamic (explicit) dispatch through pattern-matching" (p. 11:26). No other paper on soundness with multiple dispatch, reified generics and multiple inheritance together was found.

## 5. Other languages with generics and one generic interface twice

- **Java** forbids it: "different parameterizations of the same generic interface … This requirement was introduced in order to support translation by type erasure" (JLS SE 21 §8.1.5, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-8.html). The reason is erasure, not dispatch. The OOPSLA paper's "it is already required in Java" (`exclusion.tick:154-156`) borrows the rule without that reason.
- **C#** (reified) allows it except where two instantiations "may unify for some type parameter substitutions" (CS0695, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/misc/cs0695). Overloads are resolved statically: "Overload resolution is a binding-time mechanism" (§12.6.4.1), and "Static binding takes place at compile-time", except for `dynamic` (§12.3.2) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions).
- **F#** 5 added it: "You can now implement the same interface at different generic instantiations" (RFC FS-1031, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fsharp/whats-new/fsharp-50).
- **Swift** has no generic protocols, and the Generics Manifesto files them under "Unlikely": "Implicit in this feature is the ability for a given type to conform to the protocol in two different ways" (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/docs/GenericsManifesto.md, "Generic protocols").
- **Rust** allows `impl From<u8> for u64` beside `impl From<u16> for u64` (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u64.html) and forbids only overlap: "Two trait implementations overlap when … the implementations can be instantiated with the same type" (Reference, "Trait implementation coherence", https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html).
- **Kotlin** forbids it: the supertype closure must be "consistent, i.e., does not contain two parameterized types with different type arguments" (https://kotlinlang.org/spec/type-system.html, "Simple classifier types").
- **Scala** refuses it with "illegal inheritance; … inherits different type instances of trait" (compiler message, https://www.scala-lang.org/old/node/3423). No sentence found in SLS 2.13 ch. 5.
- **Haskell** allows one instance per class and type: "A type may not be declared as an instance of a particular class more than once in the program" (Haskell 2010 §4.3.2, https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch4.html). Instances are resolved statically.
- **C++** templates instantiate distinct classes, and overload resolution selects from "a list of expressions that are to be the arguments of the call" (https://eel.is/c++draft/over.match.general). Nothing selects by instantiation at run time.
- **Ceylon** (reified, multiple interface inheritance, declaration-site variance; "Like C#, and unlike Java, Ceylon's type system is fully reified") keeps the exclusion for invariant parameters and relaxes the variant ones: "for every invariant type parameter T of Y, the type argument A … given in V and … B … given in W must be exactly the same type, and, furthermore, X is a subtype of an instantiation U of Y such that U is a subtype of V&W" (spec §3.7.2 "Principal instantiation inheritance", mirror http://lucaswerkmeister.github.io/ceylon-spec/html_single/). It has no overloading at all: "Overloading is illegal in Ceylon" (§3.2.1).

## 6. The self-typed algebra tower

- Greenman, Muehlboeck, Tate (*Getting F-Bounded Polymorphism into Shape*, PLDI 2014, doi:10.1145/2594291.2594308, https://users.cs.utah.edu/~blg/publications/fbound/effing-bound-polymorphism.pdf) identify the pattern. Self-typed traits are "shapes", and "The primary one is to encode a form of self types … useful for binary methods … as well as algebraic operations, such as addition" (p. 3). Their numeric example: with Integer only `Summable<Integer>` and Float only `Summable<Float>`, "the join of Integer and Float does not exist"; under Material-Shape Separation "Summable is only permitted in inheritance and type-variable constraints, not as the type of an expression" (p. 7). A survey of 13.5 million lines of Java found no overlap (abstract), and the Ceylon team found one counterexample and planned adoption (p. 5). The paper does not treat dispatch. It names "type families" (family polymorphism) as the second use of shapes, not the tower.
- The flat encodings in current use:
  - C#: `public interface INumber<TSelf> … where TSelf : INumber<TSelf>`, implemented separately by `Int32` and `Int64` (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.numerics.inumber-1).
  - Swift: generic heterogeneous operators `static func < <Other : BinaryInteger>(lhs: Self, rhs: Other) -> Bool`. The proposal "DOES NOT solve the integer promotion problem" (SE-0104, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0104-improved-integers.md).
  - Scala: type-class values `trait Numeric[T] extends Ordering[T]` and `implicit object IntIsIntegral` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scala/scala/2.13.x/src/library/scala/math/Numeric.scala, l. 221, l. 67).
  - Cecil: the algebra on the root `num` only (§4).
- Typed Racket nests the tower statically ("Integer is a subtype of Rational, which is a subtype of Real") with union types and "overloading with intersection types". It names the tower as the hard case for typed languages: "No existing typed language provides as rich a numeric hierarchy nor as many generic operations as those found in Smalltalk, Scheme, or Racket" (St-Amour et al., *Typing the Numeric Tower*, PADL 2012, pp. 1-2, 5, https://www2.ccs.neu.edu/racket/pubs/padl12-stff.pdf). It has no self-typed traits and no run-time dispatch on type arguments.
- Apart from Naden's write-up and the 2012 patents, no source was found that treats a nested tower carrying self-typed traits at each level together with run-time dispatch over reified generics.

## What the field settled and what it did not

- **Keep the rule and flatten the tower.**
  - Java, Kotlin, Scala and X10 keep the rule, with flat numeric types and widening. Java's stated reason is erasure.
  - The Fortress group kept the rule after 2012 (Welterweight 2012, POPL 2019), for "unique minimal instance" dispatch.
  - Cecil's root-only `ordered[num]` and C#'s `INumber<TSelf>` on sibling structs are two flat shapes in use.
- **Drop the rule and instantiate at the call site with no specialised overloads.**
  - C#, F#, Rust and Haskell allow multiple instantiation, and every one chooses instances and overloads statically. None has run-time dispatch over generic overloads, the one place Naden's hole opens.
  - Ceylon allows variant multiple instantiation and has no overloading.
- **Neither route.**
  - Julia avoids the trade by single inheritance and gives up static soundness ("no notion of soundness"). It keeps specialised methods and moves ambiguity to a run-time error.
  - POPL 2019 keeps both the rule and specialisation by checking the static return type at run time, the option Naden rejected.
  - The 2012 patents' "Self-types meet … must form a forest" admits the tower's chain of self-typed instantiations inside the rule, close to the review's route C. It was never published, and its test (`comprises T`) is absent from the library's `Equality`.
- **Not settled.** Nobody published a resolution of the tower conflict under run-time dispatch, or a proof that the rule is necessary; the published proofs show only that it suffices.
